lesson.title: Making Millions of Copies of One Gene: DNA Cloning
lesson.summary: DNA cloning inserts a gene of interest into a vector such as a plasmid using restriction enzymes and DNA ligase, then uses a living host cell like bacteria to make many identical, stable copies of that gene.
lesson.body:
PCR, covered in the previous section, amplifies DNA quickly through a purely enzymatic reaction in a test tube, but it works best on relatively short, well-defined sequences and does not leave behind a permanent, living copy that can be grown, expanded, or used to actually produce a protein. DNA cloning takes a different approach: instead of copying DNA chemically, it places the gene of interest inside a living cell and lets that cell's own replication machinery copy the gene indefinitely as the cell population grows, which is useful whenever a durable, expandable, or expressible copy of a gene is needed.

The process runs through several connected steps. First, the gene of interest is obtained, either cut directly out of genomic DNA using a restriction enzyme or amplified by PCR with primers designed to add restriction sites onto its ends, directly combining the two previous sections' tools. Second, a vector, most commonly a plasmid, a small circular piece of DNA that replicates independently of the main bacterial chromosome, is cut open with that same restriction enzyme, which generates matching sticky ends on both the vector and the insert. Third, the cut insert and cut vector are mixed together with DNA ligase, an enzyme that seals breaks in the DNA backbone by forming new phosphodiester bonds; the complementary sticky ends base pair with each other, and ligase permanently joins the insert into the vector, producing a single recombinant plasmid. Fourth, that recombinant plasmid is introduced into a host cell, most often the bacterium E. coli, through a process called transformation, in which the cells are made briefly permeable so they take up the plasmid DNA. Fifth, because most plasmids carry a gene for antibiotic resistance, growing the transformed bacteria on a medium containing that antibiotic selects for only the cells that successfully took up the plasmid. Finally, as the surviving bacteria grow and divide, each cell division copies the plasmid right along with the bacterial chromosome, producing an expanding colony in which every single cell carries an identical copy, a clone, of the original gene of interest.

The practical payoff of this workflow is significant: once a gene is cloned this way, it can be sequenced and studied in essentially unlimited quantity, or, if it is placed next to a working promoter, the host cells can be induced to express it and produce large amounts of the protein it encodes.
